terms.title: ARV
terms.definition: The realistic market value of a property once all renovations, structural corrections, and finishes are executed to neighborhood standard.
terms.example: A home bought for $380,000 requiring $65,000 in work has a projected ARV of $540,000 based on recent sales within 1 mile.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio Underwrite card and Deal of the Day analysis.

terms.title: 70% Rule
terms.definition: A flipper's benchmark calculating maximum allowable offer: ARV × 70% minus estimated rehab, leaving 30% for closing, holding, and profit.
terms.example: At a $500,000 ARV with $50,000 rehab, your max offer is $300,000 ($500K × 0.70 − $50K).
terms.appPointer: Flip strategy underwrite card and Deal of the Day verdict.

terms.title: Cap Rate
terms.definition: Annual net operating income divided by purchase price or market value, measuring unleveraged yield.
terms.example: A fourplex generating $48,000 annual NOI purchased for $600,000 trades at an 8.0% cap rate.
terms.appPointer: Rental strategy returns and portfolio analytics.

terms.title: Cash-on-Cash
terms.definition: Annual pre-tax cash flow divided by total liquid capital invested (down payment, closing costs, and out-of-pocket rehab).
terms.example: Investing $85,000 cash to generate $8,500 in net annual post-debt cash flow yields a 10.0% cash-on-cash return.
terms.appPointer: Rental underwrite return breakdown and BRRRR capital recycled summary.

terms.title: DSCR
terms.definition: Monthly net operating income divided by monthly debt service (principal and interest), determining whether rental income covers the mortgage.
terms.example: A property earning $3,000 gross rent with $500 operating expenses leaves $2,500 NOI; against a $1,800 mortgage, DSCR is 1.39.
terms.appPointer: Rental underwrite loan panel and cash-flow schedule.

terms.title: NOI
terms.definition: Gross revenue minus operating expenses (taxes, insurance, maintenance, property management, and vacancy reserves), excluding debt service.
terms.example: $42,000 in gross annual rent minus $14,000 operating expenses produces a $28,000 NOI.
terms.appPointer: Rental cash-flow breakdown and cap rate calculations.

terms.title: LTV
terms.definition: The loan balance expressed as a percentage of the property’s appraised value or purchase price.
terms.example: Borrowing $360,000 on a $450,000 home purchase represents an 80% LTV.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio loan selector (Conventional, FHA, Hard Money) and BRRRR refinance calculator.

terms.title: BRRRR
terms.definition: Acquiring distressed real estate, renovating to force equity, tenanting, and executing a cash-out refinance to pull out original capital.
terms.example: Buying for $200K, rehabbing for $50K ($250K total), and refinancing 75% of a $360K ARV pulls out $270K, returning 100% of invested capital.
terms.appPointer: BRRRR strategy tab in Investor Studio.

terms.title: Comps
terms.definition: Recently sold nearby properties with similar square footage, age, and construction type used to establish fair market value.
terms.example: Three renovated 3-bed ranches sold within 0.5 miles for an average of $385/sf, establishing our valuation baseline.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio Suggested Comps panel and County Comps search.

terms.title: Just Value
terms.definition: The statutory market value determined by the Florida county property appraiser for annual ad valorem tax assessments.
terms.example: A home listing for $620,000 may carry a county Just Value of $480,000, signaling lower current tax liability.
terms.appPointer: Parcel Site Info header and Broward County tax summary.

terms.title: Qualified Sale
terms.definition: A real estate transfer between unrelated, willing parties acting in their own self-interest, certified by the county as representative of true market value.
terms.example: Sales coded 01 in Broward county records filter out family transfers, quitclaims, and foreclosure repossessions.
terms.appPointer: Deal of the Day market sales filter and county comp qualification.

terms.title: PITI
terms.definition: The complete four-component monthly carrying cost of homeownership financed through a standard mortgage.
terms.example: $2,200 principal and interest + $580 property taxes + $320 hazard insurance equals a $3,100 monthly PITI obligation.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio monthly expenses schedule and Cash-to-Close breakdown.

terms.title: PMI
terms.definition: A monthly premium charged on conventional loans when putting down less than 20% equity to protect the lender against default.
terms.example: Putting 5% down on a $400,000 purchase adds roughly $180/month in PMI until the mortgage reaches 80% LTV.
terms.appPointer: Underwrite loan inputs (toggled on for conventional loans under 20% down).

terms.title: Escrow
terms.definition: A lender-managed reserve holding borrower funds for upcoming annual property taxes, hazard insurance, and flood insurance payments.
terms.example: Lenders typically collect 3 months of taxes and 14 months of insurance upfront at closing to fund the initial escrow buffer.
terms.appPointer: Closing costs and cash-to-close card under Prepaids.

terms.title: Doc Stamps
terms.definition: State excise taxes levied on recorded Florida deeds ($0.70 per $100 in Broward/FL) and recorded mortgages ($0.35 per $100).
terms.example: On a $400,000 purchase with a $300,000 mortgage, deed stamps cost $2,800 and mortgage stamps cost $1,050.
terms.appPointer: Closing costs itemized breakdown and cash-to-close card.

terms.title: Intangible Tax
terms.definition: A one-time Florida state tax of 2 mills (0.2%, or $2 per $1,000) levied on the principal amount of all newly recorded mortgages.
terms.example: Securing a $350,000 purchase loan triggers a $700 nonrecurring intangible tax at closing.
terms.appPointer: Loan origination fees in Investor Studio closing breakdown.

terms.title: Wind Mitigation
terms.definition: A certified inspection documenting hurricane-resistant structural features (roof shape, clips/straps, opening protection) that yield significant insurance discounts.
terms.example: Having third-nail roof straps and hurricane impact windows can reduce a South Florida insurance premium from $6,500 to $3,200 annually.
terms.appPointer: Parcel Site Info inspection checklist and insurance underwrite inputs.

terms.title: 4-Point Inspection
terms.definition: A visual assessment of electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and roofing required by insurers for Florida homes over 20–30 years old.
terms.example: Insurance will be denied if the inspection uncovers an active Zinsco electrical panel, polybutylene plumbing, or a roof over 15 years old.
terms.appPointer: Property overview condition checks and roof year alert.

terms.title: FEMA 50% Rule
terms.definition: In flood zones AE and VE, if renovation costs equal or exceed 50% of the building's pre-improvement market value, the entire structure must be brought to current elevation code.
terms.example: A house with a $150,000 structural value cannot take more than $74,999 in permitted work without mandatory elevation.
terms.appPointer: Parcel Site Info flood risk warnings for SFHA / AE zones.

terms.title: Flood Zone AE vs. X
terms.fullName: FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map Zones
terms.definition: Zone AE indicates high 100-year flood risk (SFHA) requiring mandatory lender flood insurance; Zone X designates minimal risk where insurance is optional.
terms.example: A Zone AE home in Fort Lauderdale may require $2,800/yr in NFIP flood insurance, while Zone X costs $600/yr for voluntary preferred risk coverage.
terms.appPointer: Parcel Site Info flood zone tag and underwrite annual flood insurance input.

terms.title: BFE
terms.definition: The elevation surface water is expected to reach during a 100-year base flood, dictating minimum finished floor height for new construction and substantial rehab.
terms.example: If the BFE is +7.0 feet NAVD88 and the finished floor is at +5.5 feet, the structure is 1.5 feet below base flood, driving insurance premiums up.
terms.appPointer: Parcel Site Info FEMA elevation metrics.

terms.title: SFHA
terms.definition: Land within the 100-year floodplain (zones A, AE, AH, AO, VE) having at least a 1% annual chance of inundation, mandating flood insurance on federally-backed loans.
terms.example: Properties flagged SFHA = true in county GIS data require proof of flood policy prior to clear-to-close.
terms.appPointer: Parcel Site Info SFHA badge.

terms.title: Zoning
terms.definition: Local land-use regulations dictating permissible building uses, density, building heights, setbacks, and accessory dwelling unit allowances.
terms.example: A parcel zoned RS-8 allows only single-family residential with 8,000 sqft minimum lot sizes, preventing duplex conversion.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio property details and city zoning link.

terms.title: Setbacks
terms.definition: The required minimum distance between a building wall and property boundary lines established by municipal zoning ordinances.
terms.example: A 25-foot front setback and 10-foot side setback prevent building an attached garage expansion across the side property line.
terms.appPointer: Designer Hub exterior floor planning and zoning overview.

terms.title: FAR
terms.definition: The ratio of a building’s total usable floor area relative to the total square footage of the lot it sits on, capping buildable mass.
terms.example: On a 6,000 sqft lot with a 0.50 FAR cap, the maximum allowable enclosed interior space across all stories is 3,000 sqft.
terms.appPointer: Zoning calculations for expansion and ADU additions.

terms.title: Hard Money Loan
terms.definition: A short-term, asset-backed loan funded by private investors with interest-only payments, higher rates (10–12%), and 1–3 origination points used for rapid acquisition and rehab.
terms.example: Borrowing $320,000 at 10.5% interest-only for 6 months allows closing within 10 days before refinancing into permanent conventional debt.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio loan selector under 'Hard money'.

terms.title: Holding Costs
terms.definition: The cumulative monthly recurring expenses incurred while renovating a property prior to sale or lease (loan interest, taxes, insurance, utilities, HOA).
terms.example: At $3,200/month across a 6-month flip timeline, holding costs siphon $19,200 from net profit.
terms.appPointer: Flip underwrite total holding cost schedule and timeline slider.

terms.title: Seller Credits
terms.definition: Funds credited from the seller to the buyer at closing to offset buyer closing costs, prepaids, or minor inspection repairs.
terms.example: Negotiating a $10,000 seller credit directly reduces cash-to-close from $85,000 down to $75,000.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio purchase setup under Seller credits.

terms.title: Earnest Money
terms.definition: A deposit made by the buyer to the title escrow agent upon signing the purchase contract to demonstrate good-faith intent to close.
terms.example: Placing a 1% deposit ($5,000 on a $500,000 offer) holds the contract during the 10-day inspection period.
terms.appPointer: Purchase contract setup and cash-to-close ledger.

terms.title: Title Insurance
terms.definition: An insurance policy protecting against past liens, encumbrances, forgery, or defects in the chain of ownership prior to transfer.
terms.example: In Broward and Miami-Dade, the buyer traditionally chooses the title agent and pays the owner's title policy premium.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio 'Owner title paid by buyer' toggle.

terms.title: Assignment
terms.definition: A legal transfer of purchasing rights from the original contract buyer to an end buyer in exchange for an assignment fee.
terms.example: Putting a house under contract for $240,000 and assigning the contract to a rehabber for $260,000 yields a $20,000 assignment fee.
terms.appPointer: Wholesale and off-market acquisition underwriting.

terms.title: Due Diligence
terms.definition: A negotiated timeframe (typically 7–15 days) during which the buyer conducts inspections, contractor bids, and zoning checks with right of cancellation.
terms.example: Canceling on day 8 after scoping a collapsed sewer line preserves your full earnest money deposit.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio deal tracking milestones and inspection checklist.

terms.title: Contingency
terms.definition: A dedicated buffer reserved in the rehab budget to absorb unforeseen structural, electrical, or plumbing discoveries after demolition.
terms.example: On a $60,000 base scope, adding a 10% contingency reserves $6,000 for concealed termite damage or ungrounded wiring.
terms.appPointer: Designer Hub budget summary contingency line.

terms.title: Scope of Work
terms.definition: A line-item document detailing materials, labor specifications, architectural finishes, and structural milestones required for contractor bidding.
terms.example: Itemizing 12 architectural categories (demo, framing, MEP, finishes) prevents scope creep and contractor change orders.
terms.appPointer: Designer Hub itemized room expense ledger and category breakdown.

terms.title: As-Is Contract
terms.fullName: Florida Bar / Florida Realtors 'As-Is' Residential Contract
terms.definition: A standard contract where the seller makes no repair warranties, but the buyer maintains the unilateral right to inspect and cancel during due diligence.
terms.example: Submitting on an As-Is form provides a clean offer attractive to sellers while keeping earnest money safe until inspection sign-off.
terms.appPointer: Distressed property offer submission workflow.

terms.title: Lien Search
terms.definition: An inquiry with local municipalities checking for unrecorded utility liens, code compliance fines, open permits, or expired building permits.
terms.example: A municipal lien search uncovers an expired 2018 reroof permit that must be closed out before title transfer.
terms.appPointer: Closing costs itemized breakdown and parcel jurisdiction info.

terms.title: Forced Appreciation
terms.definition: Increasing real estate value through intentional renovations, square footage additions, or NOI improvements rather than relying on market inflation.
terms.example: Adding an ensuite primary bathroom and modernizing kitchen layout forces $90,000 in equity on a $42,000 spend.
terms.appPointer: Designer Hub room board planning and Underwrite ROI calculations.

terms.title: Breakeven Occ
terms.definition: The occupancy percentage a rental property must sustain so gross rents cover all operating expenses and debt service.
terms.example: A small multifamily building requiring $7,200/mo to service debt and expenses against $9,000 potential gross rent has an 80% breakeven occupancy.
terms.appPointer: Rental sensitivity analysis and stress-test card.

terms.title: Debt Yield
terms.definition: Annual NOI divided by the total loan amount, showing the lender's cash-on-cash return if they took over the asset upon foreclosure.
terms.example: A property generating $45,000 NOI with a $450,000 loan balance carries a 10.0% debt yield.
terms.appPointer: Portfolio financing and commercial DSCR loan underwriting.

terms.title: Exit Strategy
terms.definition: The planned method for monetizing or refinancing a real estate acquisition (retail flip, long-term rental hold, or cash-out refi).
terms.example: Underwriting both a retail flip exit and a rental fallback ensures you never buy a property with only one narrow path to profit.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio strategy selector (Flip, Rental, BRRRR).

terms.title: CIA / CBS & 15/25 Rule
terms.fullName: Sales Comparison Contributory Adjustments & Fannie Mae Guidelines
terms.definition: Appraisers adjust Comparable Sales—never the Subject—using market contributory value (30%–45% marginal GLA $/sf in South Florida, scaled by tier). CIA (Comp Inferior) adds value (+); CBS (Comp Better) subtracts value (−). Fannie Mae flags comps exceeding 15% Net or 25% Gross adjustments.
terms.example: Against a 2,200 sf subject with a pool, a 2,000 sf comp sold at $460K without a pool receives +$17K GLA and +$25K pool (+$42K / 9.1% Net), indicating $502K Adjusted Sale Price.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio → Value & Comps Appraisal Grid, Reconciliation Weights, and Checks card.

terms.title: FHA in plain words
terms.definition: An FHA loan lets owner-occupants buy a 1–4 unit primary residence with as little as 3.5% down (580+ credit; 10% down for 500–579). You pay a 1.75% Upfront Mortgage Insurance Premium (UFMIP, typically rolled into the loan) plus 0.55%/yr annual MIP (0.75%/yr above $726,200) that stays for the life of the loan when putting under 10% down. You must move in within 60 days and intend to live there at least 1 year; dated C5–C6 properties can pair FHA with a Limited 203(k) (up to $75,000 rehab) or Standard 203(k). Estimate for planning — confirm with your lender and CPA.
terms.example: On a $500,000 Broward single-family home (under the $667,000 1-unit FHA limit), 3.5% down is $17,500; the $482,500 base loan adds $8,444 financed UFMIP for a $490,944 total loan.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio → Deal tab → Live-in (FHA) → 01 Buy & My Buying Profile FHA limits.

terms.title: Live-in flip vs. house hack
terms.fullName: Single-Family Value-Add vs. 2–4 Unit Owner-Occupied Offset
terms.definition: A live-in flip focuses on buying an under-improved home, renovating while you live in it over 1–2 years, and capturing forced equity through a tax-advantaged sale or conventional refinance. A house hack buys 2–4 units (duplex, triplex, or fourplex) under FHA, living in one unit while renting the others—where lenders typically count 75% of the other units' market rent toward qualifying and offsetting your monthly PITI + MIP. Generally, borrowers can hold only one FHA loan at a time. Estimate for planning — confirm with your lender and CPA.
terms.example: Living in half of a $560,000 duplex where Unit B rents for $2,200/mo offsets $1,650/mo (75%) of your housing cost, often making ownership cheaper per month than renting an apartment.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio → Deal tab → Live-in (FHA) → 02 Live, 03 Improve & 04 Exit.

terms.title: Why year 2 matters (Section 121)
terms.fullName: IRS Section 121 Primary Residence Capital Gain Exclusion (2-of-5-Year Rule)
terms.definition: Under IRS Section 121, if you own and use a home as your primary residence for at least 24 months (2 years) out of the 5 years before selling, you can exclude up to $250,000 of capital gains if single or up to $500,000 if married filing jointly. Selling after only 1 year generally forfeits the full exclusion (absent specific IRS exceptions) and exposes gains to capital gains tax; renting the home out too long beyond year 5 or claiming depreciation also triggers recapture rules. Estimate for planning — confirm with your lender and CPA.
terms.example: Buying at $460,000, investing $45,000 in renovations, and netting $615,000 after selling costs creates a ~$110,000 gain—potentially $0 federal capital gains tax after 2 full years of primary occupancy vs. taxable if sold at month 12 (estimate — confirm with a CPA).
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio → Deal tab → Live-in (FHA) → 04 Exit (Scenario B: Sell 1 yr vs. 2 yrs).

terms.title: Homestead and what changes when you rent
terms.fullName: Florida Homestead Exemption, Save Our Homes Cap & Rental Reassessment
terms.definition: While a Florida home is your primary residence (as of Jan 1), Homestead Exemption reduces taxable value by up to $50,000 ($25k all levies + $25k non-school levies) and the Save Our Homes cap limits assessed value increases to 3%/yr. Once you move out and rent the property, you must notify the County Property Appraiser: you lose the Homestead Exemption and the 3% cap, and on the next assessment roll the property resets to full market value multiplied by the county millage rate (subject afterward to a 10% non-school cap). Always underwrite Exit A with non-homestead reassessed taxes! Estimate for planning — confirm with your lender and CPA.
terms.example: A Broward home bought at $420,000 and renovated to $510,000 might carry ~$7,400/yr homesteaded taxes while you live there, then jump to ~$9,945/yr (+$212/mo) at 19.5 mills once converted to a rental.
terms.appPointer: Investor Studio → Deal tab → Live-in (FHA) → Rental Phase Homestead vs. Non-Homestead Tax callout.

principles.title: The 60-30-10 Rule
principles.definition: A classic proportion framework balancing 60% dominant base canvas, 30% structural depth, and 10% high-intent accent.
principles.example: Toasted cream plaster walls and rugs (60%), espresso timber joinery and armchairs (30%), quietude blue ceramics and velvet pillows (10%).

principles.title: Scale & Proportion
principles.definition: The dimensional harmony between individual furniture volumes and the room's overarching architectural envelope.
principles.example: Placing a low 96-inch credenza with one oversized 50-inch canvas in an 11-foot ceiling salon rather than scattered smaller frames.

principles.title: Layered Lighting
principles.definition: Composing three distinct light tiers—ambient, task, and accent—to establish spatial depth and eliminate harsh overhead glare.
principles.example: Warm perimeter ceiling wash (ambient), patinated brass task sconces (task), and a low uplight behind a floor urn (accent).

principles.title: Architectural Focal Point
principles.definition: Establishing one dominant structural element that commands the eye upon entry, around which secondary furniture is composed.
principles.example: Aligning the primary seating axis around a monolithic fluted plaster fireplace flanked by low limestone bench plinths.

principles.title: Texture Contrast
principles.definition: Juxtaposing coarse, honed, and reflective materials to create tactile interest within a restrained monochromatic palette.
principles.example: Pairing slubbed raw linen drapes with smooth honed travertine tables and dark patinated bronze hardware.

principles.title: The Rule of Three
principles.definition: Arranging objects in odd-numbered groupings to create dynamic visual movement that feels organic rather than rigid.
principles.example: Styling a stone console with one tall ribbed ceramic urn, a low stacked art book, and a solid bronze match striker.

principles.title: Negative Space
principles.definition: Leaving intentional unadorned areas of floor or wall to give architectural forms room to breathe.
principles.example: Leaving six feet of bare cream plaster beside a solitary potted palm instead of hanging gallery art.

principles.title: Rhythm & Repetition
principles.definition: Carrying selected architectural details, finishes, or forms across rooms to create a continuous spatial journey.
principles.example: Repeating the gentle arched opening from the front foyer in the dining niche and primary bath mirrors.

principles.title: Compression & Release
principles.definition: Transitioning between intimate, lower-ceilinged entry thresholds and expansive, sunlit destination spaces to heighten spatial drama.
principles.example: Moving from a narrow, espresso-paneled vestibule into a soaring 14-foot ceiling courtyard pavilion.

principles.title: Sightline Alignment
principles.definition: Orienting corridors, doors, and furniture so primary pathways terminate at natural light, exterior greenery, or architectural art.
principles.example: Aligning the central hallway corridor directly with an outdoor reflecting pool through floor-to-ceiling glass.

principles.title: Color Temperature (Kelvin)
principles.definition: Calibrating light bulb warmth (2700K vs. 3000K) to complement warm plaster and wood grains without sterile blue spikes.
principles.example: Using 2700K warm-dim LEDs in living rooms to turn cream walls golden at dusk while reserving 3000K for task vanity mirrors.

principles.title: Spatial Balance
principles.definition: Equilibrating visual weight across an axis through either formal symmetry or informal, sculptural asymmetry.
principles.example: Balancing a massive dark oak bookcase on the left wall with a pair of deep lounge chairs and an oversized floor lamp on the right.

principles.title: Visual Weight
principles.definition: How heavily an object draws the eye based on its color darkness, material density, pattern complexity, and scale.
principles.example: A dark espresso solid-base pedestal table carries more visual gravity than an identical-sized glass top on brass hairpin legs.

principles.title: Harmony & Unity
principles.definition: Ensuring all architectural finishes, fabrics, and metal accents share an underlying tonal affinity that reads as one cohesive vision.
principles.example: Anchoring hardware across the entire main floor in unlacquered brass so kitchens, powder baths, and built-ins feel unified.

principles.title: Threshold Framing
principles.definition: Designing doorways and casing profiles as visual frames that compose painterly views into adjoining rooms.
principles.example: Framing a deep green dining room through a wide, casing-free arched portal cut into a sunlit cream living room.

principles.title: Finish Tactility
principles.definition: Selecting honed, wire-brushed, or tumbled finishes that invite touch and diffuse light naturally rather than reflecting artificial sheen.
principles.example: Specifying a honed matte marble island countertop over high-gloss polished stone for softer reflections and understated luxury.

principles.title: Ceiling Height Illusion
principles.definition: Using floor-to-ceiling drapery, full-height doors, and low-profile horizontal seating to draw the eye upward and exaggerate volume.
principles.example: Hanging linen drapery tracks directly against the ceiling crown rather than the window casing to visually lift an 8-foot ceiling.

principles.title: Acoustic Softening
principles.definition: Balancing hard reflective planes (tile, plaster, glass) with plush acoustic absorption (wool rugs, drapery, bouclé, upholstery) to dampen echo.
principles.example: Placing an expansive thick wool-pile area rug and heavy pleated linen panels in a limestone dining room to make dinner conversation intimate.

principles.title: Organic Imperfection
principles.definition: Incorporating artisanal hand-thrown ceramics, raw edges, and natural grain variations to prevent modern minimalism from feeling clinical.
principles.example: Centering a hand-carved solid suar wood bench with natural edge checking in a sleek, minimalist plaster entry hall.

principles.title: Biophilic Connection
principles.definition: Integrating natural daylight, organic botanicals, and raw earthy materials to foster calm well-being within interior spaces.
principles.example: Positioning an oversized clay urn holding cut olive branches directly beneath a ceiling skylight in a central atrium.

principles.title: Monochromatic Nuance
principles.definition: Building depth within a single color family by varying sheen, weave density, and minute tone shifts from cream to sand.
principles.example: Layering alabaster plaster walls, oat boucle armchairs, ivory cashmere throws, and a natural jute rug without introducing any other hue.

principles.title: Curated Material Restraint
principles.definition: Limiting a home’s primary finish palette to no more than 3 core materials across all rooms for intentional luxury.
principles.example: Restricting every surface across the property to rift-sawn white oak, Calacatta Viola marble, and unlacquered burnished brass.

principles.title: Circulation & Flow
principles.definition: Maintaining a minimum 36-inch continuous clearance corridor between major furniture pieces for effortless movement.
principles.example: Allowing 42 inches between kitchen island barstools and the dining table so two people can pass comfortably.

principles.title: Plinth Grounding
principles.definition: Using low, solid-base platform furniture and stone plinths to anchor seating firmly to the floor plane.
principles.example: Mounting a custom low oak platform beneath the sofa and credenza so furniture feels rooted rather than hovering on spindly legs.

principles.title: Light Reflectance Value (LRV)
principles.definition: The percentage of light a paint color reflects, determining how bright a room will feel under natural and artificial exposure.
principles.example: Choosing an off-white with an LRV of 74 ensures the north-facing bedroom stays luminous without glaring under morning sun.

principles.title: Spatial Hierarchy
principles.definition: Graduating importance across interconnected zones through varying ceiling heights, flooring transitions, and scale.
principles.example: Designing the primary great room with double-height volume and rich coffering while keeping adjoining hallways understated.

principles.title: Architectural Reveal
principles.definition: Introducing a subtle recessed groove or shadow line (typically 0.5 inches) where materials meet instead of applying bulky surface baseboards.
principles.example: Installing flush reglet drywall baseboards with a recessed 1/2-inch shadow line where plaster meets wide-plank oak flooring.

principles.title: Patina & Aging
principles.definition: Selecting living finishes (unlacquered brass, oiled walnut, vegetable-tanned leather) that grow richer and more characterful with daily touch.
principles.example: Installing unlacquered brass lever handles that darken to a warm, mottled bronze at contact points over years of handling.

principles.title: Concealed Storage
principles.definition: Integrating touch-latch or pocketing panel cabinetry that disguises everyday clutter as clean architectural millwork.
principles.example: Concealing a coffee station and pantry appliances behind full-height pocketing oak doors flush with the perimeter kitchen wall.

principles.title: Anchoring the Floor Plane
principles.definition: Selecting an area rug large enough so all front and rear legs of primary seating rest firmly on the weave.
principles.example: Specifying a generous 10x14-foot wool rug rather than an 8x10 so the sectional, lounge chairs, and cocktail table sit fully inside its border.

principles.title: Transitional Vignette
principles.definition: Composing small, curated moments of pause at landings, alcoves, and hallway turns to enrich the home’s secondary journey.
principles.example: Placing a petite marble pedestal with a single bronze sculpture and soft directional pin spot at the top of the stair landing.

principles.title: Natural Wood Warmth
principles.definition: Introducing authentic wood species to counter cool masonry, glass, and metals with tactile warmth and grounding organic grain.
principles.example: Wrapping ceiling beams in warm quarter-sawn white oak to balance cool large-format porcelain floor tiles.

principles.title: Contrast of Mass and Void
principles.definition: Balancing solid, heavy architectural volumes with transparent openings, floating plinths, and negative voids.
principles.example: Cantilevering a heavy stone vanity over an open, illuminated floor gap to keep the powder room feeling weightless.

principles.title: Ambient Wash
principles.definition: Grazing architectural walls with soft, indirect perimeter lighting to emphasize plaster texture without visible bulb glare.
principles.example: Concealing a continuous warm LED cove tape inside a ceiling drop to wash textured Roman clay plaster in gentle diffused glow.

principles.title: Scale Juxtaposition
principles.definition: Pairing unexpectedly large focal objects with delicate minimal accents to create deliberate editorial tension.
principles.example: Suspending a dramatic 42-inch wide ceramic pendant over a slender, low-profile two-person dining banquette.

principles.title: Tonal Graduation
principles.definition: Progressively shifting values from dark to light as sightlines travel from floor to ceiling to maximize perceived headroom.
principles.example: Deep espresso hardwood floors anchoring the base, mid-tone oat furniture at eye level, and ethereal toasted cream ceilings overhead.

principles.title: Directional Flooring Lay
principles.definition: Running hardwood planks or large stone pavers parallel to primary natural light sources to visually extend room length.
principles.example: Orienting wide-plank oak flooring perpendicular to the front door so plank lines guide the eye toward rear garden sliders.

principles.title: Hardware Consistency
principles.definition: Maintaining a disciplined standard of metal weights, finishes, and profiles across doors, cabinets, and drapery rods.
principles.example: Standardizing all interior door levers in solid knurled burnished brass matching the cabinet pulls in the open kitchen.

principles.title: Sculptural Silhouette
principles.definition: Selecting chairs or accent pieces with expressive profiles that read as freestanding art from all 360-degree room angles.
principles.example: Floating a rounded bouclé swivel chair with a curved sculptural barrel back in the center of the room.

principles.title: Curated Asymmetry
principles.definition: Balancing disparate elements of equal visual weight on either side of an axis to avoid predictable, rigid mirror imaging.
principles.example: Flanking a king bed with a tall fluted wood cabinet on the left and a low stone cantilevered nightstand with hanging pendant on the right.
